description: Planar magnetic versus dynamic headphone drivers, explained at MSN-chat pace. A live diaphragm-motion demo: a dynamic cone driven at one point breaks up at high frequency, while a planar film driven everywhere stays flat.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. Drag the frequency in the demo above.
disclosure: Starter draft. The mechanism is standard driver physics; the demo is a real phase-lag model (a cone driven at one point against a film driven everywhere), not a measurement. Background paraphrased from Wikipedia and the usual headphone references.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader can recognize drivers vocabulary without being able to predict what its mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain drivers in plain language and predict its behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model; they do not replace a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you go, a quick check that the mechanism stuck. 4 questions, no stakes. Pick the reply you would actually send.

questions.q: Start at the top. A dynamic driver and a planar driver both turn current into force on a diaphragm. What is the actual difference between them?

options.t: where the force lands. a dynamic pushes at one point, the coil, and a planar pushes across the whole film
options.why: Right. The dynamic glues a voice coil to the cone and pushes there; the planar etches the conductor across the film so the force lands evenly over the whole surface. Everything else on this page follows from that.

options.t: the magnets. planars use big magnet arrays and dynamics use an electromagnet coil instead
options.why: Both use both. The dynamic coil sits in a magnet gap, and the planar film hangs between magnet arrays. Scroll back to the first reply: the split is where the force lands, and the rest is downstream of that.

options.t: the shapes. a cone focuses the sound outward and a flat film spreads it out evenly
options.why: The shape is a side effect. The cone needs its shape to stay stiff under a point push, and the film can be flat because the push is spread out. Point drive versus distributed drive is the load-bearing difference.

options.t: the stiffness. the planar film is more rigid, so it tracks the signal more accurately
options.why: Backwards. The planar film is famously thin and floppy, and it gets away with that because it is driven everywhere at once, so it never needs to be stiff enough to resist a point load.

questions.q: You dragged the frequency slider in the demo. What happens to the dynamic cone as the frequency climbs?

options.t: the rim starts lagging the center, since the push has to travel outward from the coil
options.why: That is the whole demo. The motion propagates out from the coil as a bending wave, the phase lag grows with frequency, and past a point the surface stops moving as one piece. It breaks into modes.

options.t: the whole cone just moves less, since it can't keep up with the faster signal
options.why: Watch the top panel again at high frequency: the cone still moves plenty. The failure is phase, with different parts of the surface falling out of step, and the ripples you see are exactly that lag.

options.t: both surfaces start rippling, the planar sheet just ripples a little less
options.why: Drag the slider and watch the bottom panel: the film stays flat at every frequency, because every point gets pushed at the same instant. There is no wave that has to travel across it.

options.t: it was breaking up at low frequency too, you just couldn't see it yet
options.why: At low frequency the wavelength inside the cone is long compared to the cone itself, so the whole thing moves as one piston either way. Breakup is specifically a high-frequency problem.

questions.q: When the cone breaks up like that, what does it do to what you actually hear?

options.t: it radiates sound that wasn't in the signal, showing up as treble resonances and distortion
options.why: Exactly. Regions moving out of step each radiate on their own, and the sum contains output the recording never asked for. That is why breakup lands as resonance peaks and extra distortion up high.

options.t: nothing much, the little ripples average out by the time the sound reaches your ear
options.why: They do not average out. Each out-of-step region radiates on its own, and the extra energy sits at frequencies the signal never contained, which is the definition of distortion.

options.t: it mostly wrecks the bass, since that's where the cone has to move the furthest
options.why: Bass is where the cone is happiest: at low frequencies it moves as one piston. Scroll back two replies, the trouble starts high, where the wavelength inside the diaphragm gets short.

options.t: the volume just drops, since the out-of-step parts cancel each other out
options.why: Some cancellation happens, but the audible signature is added coloration: resonance peaks and distortion in the treble. The extra output is the problem, because it was never in the signal.

questions.q: Last one. If spreading the drive keeps the treble cleaner, why is nearly every headphone in the world still dynamic?

options.t: planars pay in weight, size, and amp power, and dynamics do easy bass cheaply off a phone
options.why: That is the tradeoff. Planars buy low treble distortion with heavy magnet arrays, an inefficient diaphragm, and amp hunger. Dynamics move a lot of air cheaply and efficiently, which is what most listeners need.

options.t: mostly patents and habit, the industry just hasn't moved over to planars yet
options.why: The chat gave physical reasons rather than inertia: heavy magnet arrays, an inefficient flat diaphragm, and hunger for amp power. Those costs are real, so dynamics stay the sensible default.

options.t: planars can't really do deep bass, so dynamics stick around to cover the low end
options.why: The page says deep bass is simple for dynamics, which is a weaker claim than bass being impossible for planars. The planar penalty is weight, size, and efficiency; the low octaves are still reachable.

options.t: planars do always sound better, dynamics just win because they're the cheap option
options.why: The closing exchange cuts against that: the mechanism only sets tendencies. A well-engineered dynamic can beat a sloppy planar, because tuning and build decide the final result.

messages.html: planar magnetic vs dynamic drivers. audiophiles talk about planars like a different species. what actually changes between them?

How the diaphragm gets pushed. A dynamic driver glues a voice coil to a cone and parks it in a magnet gap; current through the coil makes a force at that one spot, and the cone has to carry that push out to its edges. A planar driver etches the conductor across a thin flat film hung between two magnet arrays, so the force lands evenly over the whole surface.
so one pushes at a point, the other pushes everywhere. why does that matter?

At low frequencies it barely does; the cone moves as one piston either way. The split shows up high, where the wavelength inside the diaphragm gets short. A point-driven cone has to propagate that motion outward, so the rim starts lagging the center and the surface stops moving as one piece. It breaks into modes. The flat film, driven everywhere at once, stays flat.

demo.bar: watch the diaphragm move · drag the frequency
demo.html: Top: a dynamic cone driven at one point (the voice coil, the dark bar at the center). Bottom: a planar membrane driven evenly across its area (the row of bars). Drag the frequency: the cone's rim lags its center and the surface breaks up, while the planar sheet stays flat.

messages.html: so those ripples in the top one are the cone breaking up. that's distortion?

It is. When different parts of the diaphragm move out of step, they radiate sound that was not in the signal, which shows up as resonance peaks and extra distortion in the treble. Spreading the drive is how planars keep distortion low up high. It is also why a planar diaphragm can be so thin and light: it never has to be stiff enough to stay rigid under a point load.
if planars are cleaner, why isn't everything planar?

Tradeoffs. Those magnet arrays are heavy and the big flat diaphragm is inefficient, so planars tend to be bigger, heavier on your head, and hungry for amp power. Dynamic drivers are light, cheap, efficient, and move a lot of air easily, which makes deep bass simple and lets them run off a phone. Most headphones in the world are dynamic for exactly those reasons.
so planar trades weight and power for low distortion, and dynamic trades some treble cleanliness for efficiency and easy bass.

That is the honest summary. Neither wins outright. A well-engineered dynamic driver can sound excellent, and a sloppy planar can sound worse than a good dynamic. The mechanism sets the tendencies; the tuning and the build decide the result.
